findings.claim: Nine questions are typed '2 marks - State' (L1 q2, L5 q2, L7 q2, L8 q2, L9 q2, L10 q2, L13 q2, L14 q6, L15 q2). L14 q6 also opens 'Identify two documents...' while typed as State.
findings.truth: On this paper State, Give, Identify and Define are all 1-mark command words; the 2-mark slot is Outline, defined as two linked points about one business concept placed in context. Each question is reshaped to ask for one item plus a linked development, and the mark scheme is rewritten as 1 + 1.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Outline = give two linked points; State = an answer no longer than a sentence)

findings.claim: Fourteen questions are typed '3 marks - Outline' (every lesson except L11). Eight of them ask for two things at once, e.g. 'Outline one advantage and one disadvantage of a business choosing external (inorganic) growth through a takeover.'
findings.truth: Outline is worth 2 marks. The 3-mark command word is Explain: a statement of fact with two further expansion points. The label becomes Explain in all fourteen. Where the stem asked for two separate things, which no 3-mark command word supports, it is cut to one point and the scheme rewritten as 1 + 1 + 1 - the shape the existing schemes already used.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Explain = a statement of fact with two further expansion points)

findings.claim: Nine questions are typed '6 marks - Explain' (L1 q4, L2 q3, L4 q3, L5 q4, L7 q4, L9 q4, L10 q4, L13 q4, L14 q3), each with a four-band level ladder sized for 6 marks.
findings.truth: Explain is a 3-mark short answer. A 6-mark extended answer with no context is Discuss. The tariff and the ladder are right, so only the command word and the stem verb change.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Discuss = an extended answer, no context in the question)

findings.claim: Fifteen questions are typed '9 marks - Discuss' or '9 marks - Analyse in Context', with ladders running 8-9 / 5-7 / 3-4 / 1-2 (L1 q5, L2 q4, L2 q6, L3 q5, L4 q4, L5 q5, L6 q5, L7 q5, L8 q5, L9 q5, L10 q5, L12 q5, L13 q5, L14 q4, L15 q5).
findings.truth: Discuss and Analyse are both 6-mark questions on this paper; the 9-mark question is Justify. The stems are correctly worded Discuss and Analyse tasks, so the tariff drops to 6 and the ladder is rescaled to 5-6 / 3-4 / 2 / 1.
findings.evidence: spec Theme 2 assessment overview (Section A 35, Section B 30, Section C 25) and Appendix 1 command word taxonomy

findings.claim: Ten questions are typed '12 marks - Justify a Recommendation', each presenting two options and asking the student to recommend one (L1 q6, L3 q6, L4 q6, L5 q6, L6 q6, L8 q6, L9 q6, L11 q6, L13 q6, L15 q6).
findings.truth: Justify is the 9-mark question; 12 marks is Evaluate. These stems are textbook Justify tasks - two options, recommend one - so the tariff drops to 9 and the ladder rescales to 8-9 / 5-7 / 3-4 / 1-2. The alternative, keeping 12 marks and rewriting each stem into a single-proposition Evaluate question, was rejected because it would discard the two-option framing the whole mark scheme is built on.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Justify = use information provided to recommend one of two options; Evaluate = reach a supported conclusion about a business situation)

findings.claim: Thirteen exam tips and three passages of body text teach the same impossible tariffs ('6-mark Explain', '9-mark Discuss', '9-mark Analyse in Context', '12-mark Justify', 'Outline questions (3 marks)'), and several make claims the board does not publish: 'the examiner wants to see', 'examiners want you to', 'the examiner credits the best two only', 'Examiners want to see candidates recognise', 'Pearson has signalled this topic as a priority for extended evaluation', and a rule that you must use context 'at least twice to score in the upper tier'.
findings.truth: Tariffs corrected to the real ladder (1 / 2 / 3 / 6 / 9 / 12). The invented examiner and board claims are replaced with neutral advice that keeps the underlying point.
findings.evidence: spec Theme 2 assessment overview and Appendix 1; no Pearson publication makes any of the quoted claims

findings.claim: 'the re-order level is set above minimum stock to account for lead time, and the gap between them is the buffer stock'
findings.truth: Buffer stock IS the minimum stock level, not the gap above it. The lesson body says so ('Minimum stock level (buffer stock)') and practice question 1 marks 150 units correct for a graph with a 400 re-order level and a 150 minimum. The conclusion contradicted both.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3.2 (interpretation of bar gate stock graphs); internal contradiction with L9 body text and L9 q1 answer key

findings.claim: 'Flexible hours' is defined, in both the dfn tooltip and the glossary, as 'A contract that does not fix working hours in advance; the employer offers work and the employee can accept or decline.'
findings.truth: That is a zero-hours contract. The prose two lines later gives the right definition: flexible hours let employees vary start and finish times around core hours. Both the tooltip and the glossary entry are corrected to match the prose.
findings.evidence: spec 2.5.1 (part-time, full-time and flexible hours); internal contradiction with the L13 body text

findings.claim: 'Job enrichment' is defined, in both the dfn tooltip and the glossary, as 'Expanding an employee's role to include more challenging and varied tasks at a similar level of responsibility.'
findings.truth: 'More varied tasks at a similar level of responsibility' is job enlargement. Enrichment adds responsibility, which is exactly what the lesson body says ('job enrichment adds more responsibility, complexity, and challenge to a role'). A student who used the tooltip definition would describe the wrong technique.
findings.evidence: spec 2.5.4 (non-financial methods: job rotation, job enrichment, autonomy); internal contradiction with the L15 body text

findings.claim: 'After Brexit, UK businesses trading with the EU faced new customs checks, regulatory requirements and, in some sectors, tariffs that did not exist previously.'
findings.truth: The UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement gives zero tariffs and zero quotas on goods that meet the agreed rules of origin. Tariffs apply to goods that fail those rules, not to particular sectors. Rewritten so a student does not answer that Brexit put tariffs on UK-EU trade generally.
findings.evidence: UK-EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement, tariff and rules-of-origin provisions

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which production process offers the most flexibility for product changes?' answered 'Batch production - the line can be reconfigured between batches.'
findings.truth: Job production is the most flexible. The lesson body states it directly: 'Job production offers maximum flexibility and customisation at the highest cost per unit... Batch production sits in between.' The card marked the true answer wrong.
findings.evidence: spec 2.3.1 (job, batch, flow); internal contradiction with the L8 body text

findings.claim: Flashcards 1 and 2 ask the identical question, 'What does function mean in the design mix?', with near-identical answers. 'Cost', the third element of the design mix, has no card.
findings.truth: Card 2 is repurposed to cover cost, so the deck covers all three elements of the design mix once each.
findings.evidence: spec 2.2.1 (the design mix: function, aesthetics, cost)

findings.claim: The exchange-rate calculation mark scheme reads '0 marks if only working is shown without the correct final answer' and '[2 marks - answer only; working earns nothing if the answer is absent or wrong]'. L6's exam tip repeats it: 'the final numerical answer... is what earns marks'.
findings.truth: The spec tells students workings should be given, and calculation questions carry a method mark. L11's own exam tip already says so ('a method mark may be available for a correct formula'), so the unit contradicted itself. Both are corrected to award the method mark.
findings.evidence: spec Theme 2 assessment information (calculators; workings should be given) and Appendix 1 (Calculate)

findings.claim: 'Calculate the psychological price Harbour & Bloom should charge if the full price of the premium candle is 20.00 pounds', marked with 'Formula: psychological price = full price minus a small amount, typically ending in .99 or .95 (1 mark for method)'.
findings.truth: There is no such formula and psychological pricing is not a calculation - it is a judgement about how a price is perceived. Replaced with a percentage-change calculation on the two prices already in the stem (20.00 against 12.00 = 66.7% to one decimal place), which is on the spec's quantitative skills list.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 2 quantitative skills (percentages and percentage changes); recomputation 8 / 12 x 100 = 66.7%

findings.claim: The ARR question states 'total additional profit of 56,000 pounds over four years' and its mark scheme gives three different answers: it headlines '3 marks for the correct final answer of 40.00%', then works to 10.00%, then adds a note giving 35.00% and says either is acceptable.
findings.truth: 40.00% is not reachable by any reading of the data. Reading 56,000 as returns: (56,000 - 40,000) / 4 = 4,000; 4,000 / 40,000 x 100 = 10.00%. Reading it as profit: 56,000 / 4 = 14,000; 14,000 / 40,000 x 100 = 35.00%. The stem now says 'total returns', matching the lesson's own worked example, and the scheme gives one answer, 10.00%, with staged method marks.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 3 formula (ARR (%) = (average annual profit [total profit / no. of years] / cost of investment) x 100); recomputation

findings.claim: Two multi-step calculations are typed '1 mark - Identify from Data': L11 q3 needs gross profit, then net profit, then the margin; L12 q1 needs the total market, then the share. Both mark schemes print full working for a single mark.
findings.truth: Identify means selecting a value straight off a graph or table. Anything needing arithmetic is Calculate. L11 q3 becomes a 3-mark Calculate (30.00%, recomputed: 500,000 - 200,000 = 300,000; 300,000 - 140,000 - 10,000 = 150,000; 150,000 / 500,000 x 100) and L12 q1 a 2-mark Calculate (10.00%, recomputed: 4,500,000 + 40,500,000 = 45,000,000; 4,500,000 / 45,000,000 x 100). L9 q1 is left alone - the buffer stock is read straight off the graph, so Identify is right there.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Identify = select the correct answer from reading a graph or table of data); recomputation

findings.claim: L11 description is 108 characters and L12 is 104; the content validator caps descriptions at 100.
findings.truth: Both shortened without losing the topic.
findings.evidence: house validator limit

findings.claim: 'Toyota pioneered this system in the 1970s and it has since spread across many industries', repeated in a flashcard question ('Which company pioneered just-in-time stock control in the 1970s?').
findings.truth: Toyota developed just-in-time as part of the Toyota Production System from the late 1940s onwards; the 1970s is when it spread beyond Japan. The attribution to Toyota is right and no mark scheme tests the decade, so this is not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: widely published history of the Toyota Production System

findings.claim: 'High-profile pressure groups active in the UK include Greenpeace (environmental issues), Fairtrade (ethical supply chains)...'
findings.truth: The Fairtrade Foundation is primarily a certification and labelling body rather than a campaigning pressure group, though it does run public campaigns. The looseness would not cost a mark, and swapping in another named organisation risks introducing a new error.
findings.evidence: spec 2.1.4 (the potential impact of pressure group activity on the marketing mix)

findings.claim: Flashcards 5 and 6 are near-duplicates: 'Why is product knowledge an important element of the sales process?' and 'How does strong product knowledge improve a business's sales performance?', with answers that differ only in wording.
findings.truth: One wasted card in a five-card deck. Not a factual error, and the two answer strings are not identical, so the validator would pass it.
findings.evidence: internal

findings.claim: Six of the fourteen questions relabelled '3 marks - Explain' under F2 keep a case-study scenario in the stem (L5 q3, L6 q3, L7 q3, L8 q3, L9 q3, L10 q3), and their schemes award a mark for a contextual link.
findings.truth: Pearson's taxonomy says Explain questions carry no context; the contextual short answer is the 2-mark Outline. Two options. (a) Leave the context in, as done here: it costs a student nothing to write, and the schemes still work as 1 + 1 + 1. (b) Strip the scenario sentence from all six stems so they are true context-free Explain questions, and delete the contextual-link mark. My recommendation is (a) - the context makes the questions better practice for the Section B source-booklet style, and no examiner penalises a student for applying knowledge.
findings.evidence: spec Appendix 1 command word taxonomy (Explain: 'There is no context in these questions')
findings.ruling: NOTE: relabelled 3-mark Explain items keep their case-study stems; context does no harm.

findings.claim: After F15 and F16, L11's ladder is 2 / 3 / 3 / 3 / 6 / 9 - four Calculate questions and no 1-mark opener, unlike every other lesson in the unit.
findings.truth: Every real Section A opens with a 1-mark multiple-choice or Define question. Two options. (a) Leave it: this is the calculations lesson, and four calculation questions are good practice. (b) Add a 1-mark multiple-choice item on the gross-profit formula and drop one of the three 3-mark Calculate questions. My recommendation is (a) - authoring a new question is outside the scope of a fact-check, and nothing in the current set is wrong.
findings.evidence: spec Theme 2 assessment overview (paper consists of calculations, multiple-choice, short-answer and extended-writing questions)
findings.ruling: NOTE: L11 lacks a 1-mark opener after relabelling; authoring a new item is beyond a fact-check.

summary: Every lesson carries the same fault: the practice ladder uses real Edexcel tariffs (1/2/3/6/9/12) but attaches the wrong command word to five of the six rungs, and thirteen exam tips teach those impossible tariffs alongside invented examiner and board claims. Beneath that, eight substantive errors: buffer stock redefined as the gap above the minimum, flexible hours defined as a zero-hours contract, job enrichment defined as job enlargement, a flashcard marking batch production the most flexible process, an invented psychological-pricing formula, an ARR mark scheme printing three different answers with a headline figure reachable by none, two multi-step calculations tariffed at one mark, and a calculation scheme that refuses the method mark. All arithmetic elsewhere (margins, ARR, market share, percentage change) recomputed correct, and every knowledge-check answer key verified.
